newsitem.title: USA: NY Consumer Board seeks more power rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: NY Consumer Board seeks more power rate cuts.

text.p: The executive director of The New York State Consumer Protection Board would like to see more rate cuts in the settlements New York utilities are reaching with the staff of the Department of Public Service.
Timothy S. Carey characterizes the settlements as a "first step toward providing real financial relief to the small businesses and middle and low income wage earners" served by the utilities.
The state Consumer Protection Board was created by the state legislature in 1970 to speak for consumers and small businesses.

Separately, Carey praised the 20 percent rate reduction agreement announced last week by Long Island Lighting Co, Brooklyn Union Gas Co and the Long Island Power Authority, calling the settlement "an optimal resolution to the problem of high electric rates on Long Island."

He said Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp and Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc -- the three utilities that have settled with the staff -- have come a long way, pointing out they voluntarily gave up their monolopy status.

But the board does not find the restructuring settlements "acceptable at this point," Carey said, noting "concerns about the rate reductions for small customers (and the delay required) before all utility ratepayers will be able to choose from among competitive sources of electricity."

He also questioned whether or not the settlements offerred sufficient incentive for residential and small commercial power buyers to seek other electricity suppliers. To do that, Carey said, rates need to be designed to provide the potential for savings of about 10 percent rather than the three percent or so seen under the Central Hudson pact.

Citing Consumer Protection Board figures, he said Central Hudson now charges residential power users about $0.11 per kilowatt hour. The settlement will result in a base price of about $0.075 per kilowatt hour, including a $0.015 charge to cover stranded assets, which means a third party marketer would have to deliver power for $0.035 per kilowatt hour or less to compete for Central Hudson's customers.

The Con Edison settlement provides for decreases for each of the next five years of five percent for industrial customers; two percent for commercial customers; and only 0.6 percent for other customers, Carey noted.

He said the board "believes that Con Ed has the resources to provide further rate reductions. The $655 million rate reduction provided for by the settlement is in our estimation distributed inequitably."

Asked how the New York Public Service Commissin came up with its view that Con Edison was cutting its rates $1 billion over five years, Kevin Bronner, the CPB's director utility intervention, pointed out the utility already had a pending rate cut for $87 million per year.
"We're discounting that" when stating it agreed to a $655 million reduction, Bronner said.
He said the board believes Con Edison's allowed return on equity "should be closer to 10 percent," than the 12.9 percent allowed in the settlement.
The utility's rates could also be lowered by removing property held for future use from its rate base," he said.
